title: Bridging Event‐Based and StorAge Selection Approaches to Backward Travel Time Distributions
content:
Abstract

Event-based backward travel time distributions (bTTDs) inferred from environmental tracer time series provide event-scale insight into catchment transport, whereas StorAge Selection (SAS) functions describe integrated transport dynamics at the system scale. Despite their shared conceptual basis, their relationship across temporal scales remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a unified framework to directly compare event-based and SAS-derived bTTDs. Event-based bTTDs are reconstructed from environmental tracer time series and expressed in event-order space, while SAS-based bTTDs are projected onto the same representation using storage-age information. Building on this, we introduce a hybrid formulation that adaptively combines both sources of information. The framework is evaluated using controlled numerical experiments and a multi-year field tracer data set. Event-based bTTDs capture short-term variability but are sensitive to noise and incomplete responses, whereas SAS-based bTTDs provide smoother but temporally aggregated representations. In the numerical experiments, the hybrid approach consistently improves agreement with reference bTTDs, primarily through improved reconstruction of distributional shape while providing modest improvements in event-order mean travel time estimates. Additional analyses of the numerical experiments indicate that increasing the complexity of SAS representations, such as through time-varying formulations, does not necessarily improve hybrid reconstruction performance. Within the investigated model framework, stationary SAS functions provide the most robust basis for hybridization, suggesting that the SAS component primarily acts as a stabilizing system-scale constraint. These results demonstrate that event-based and SAS approaches encode complementary information and highlight the importance of balancing process detail and robustness when combining event-scale and storage-based transport models.
